title: Transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT)
subtitle: Complete resection with detrusor muscle in the specimen

sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Bladder cancer: diagnosis and management (NG2)

indications: Any bladder tumour seen at cystoscopy or on imaging: TURBT is both the diagnostic and, for non-muscle-invasive disease, the primary treatment.
Re-resection (second TURBT) after incomplete initial resection, for T1 tumours, or when no detrusor muscle was in the first specimen, as the guideline specifies.
Palliation of bleeding from a bladder tumour.
contraindications: A patient unfit for anaesthesia, where outpatient fulguration or biopsy may be the better choice for small low-grade recurrences.
preparation: Review the flexible cystoscopy findings and imaging; CT urography to assess the upper tracts.
Urine cytology where it will inform management.
Consent covers bleeding, infection, bladder perforation and its management, the possibility of further resections, intravesical treatment, and the possible diagnosis of invasive cancer.
Check that the immediate post-operative chemotherapy instillation is available if it is planned.
positioning: For lateral wall tumours, plan with the anaesthetist: general anaesthesia with neuromuscular blockade or an obturator nerve block reduces the obturator reflex.
equipment: Rigid cystoscope with 30 and 70 degree lenses; resectoscope with monopolar or bipolar loops; cold-cup biopsy forceps.
Ellik evacuator; three-way catheter and irrigation.
Enhanced cystoscopy (blue light or narrow-band imaging) where available, which improves detection of small papillary tumours and carcinoma in situ.
anatomy: The bladder wall is thin, particularly at the dome and in an elderly, distended bladder. Lateral wall resection lies close to the obturator nerve.
The dome and posterior wall are covered by peritoneum: perforation here can be intraperitoneal. The anterior and lateral walls and the bladder neck are extraperitoneal.
Ureteric orifices lie at the lateral corners of the trigone; tumours near them may involve them.
The detrusor muscle layer must be in the specimen to stage the tumour; its absence leaves stage unknown.
criticalSafety: Map every tumour (number, size, site, appearance) before the first cut, and record it as a bladder diagram.
Resect completely, including the base, and send the base as a separate specimen containing detrusor muscle.
Anticipate the obturator jerk on the lateral wall. Reduce bladder filling, use low current or bipolar energy, and ask for paralysis or an obturator nerve block.
Do not give an immediate post-operative chemotherapy instillation if a perforation is suspected or there is bleeding requiring irrigation.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel adjacent to an intraperitoneal perforation
commonErrors: A superficial resection without muscle, making the specimen unstageable.
Diathermy artefact from excessive coagulation that destroys the tissue the pathologist needs.
Overfilling the bladder, which thins the wall and increases perforation risk.
Missing small satellite tumours or carcinoma in situ by not inspecting the whole bladder.
Forgetting to plan the second resection or the instillation.
complications: Bladder perforation: most are extraperitoneal and managed with catheter drainage; intraperitoneal perforations may need laparoscopic or open repair.
Ureteric orifice injury and later obstruction.
Under-staging and early recurrence after incomplete resection.
postop: Irrigation until clear; catheter duration depends on the size of the resection and any perforation.
Immediate single post-operative intravesical chemotherapy instillation for appropriate tumours, within the window the guideline sets, when there is no perforation or significant bleeding.
Histology discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting, with risk stratification, second resection, intravesical therapy and surveillance planned from it.
Muscle-invasive disease needs staging and a radical treatment discussion.

steps.emphasis: Confirm the instillation plan at the time-out, and whether the tumour is on a lateral wall.
Lithotomy with padded stirrups; discuss neuromuscular blockade or an obturator block now if a lateral wall tumour is expected.
Draw the bladder diagram: number, size, site and appearance of every tumour, and suspicious flat areas.
Keep the exophytic tumour and the base in separate labelled pots.
Coagulate the resection edges and base at low bladder volume, sparingly, to avoid thermal injury through a thin wall.
A suspected perforation cancels the immediate chemotherapy instillation. Say so aloud and write it down.

step.turbt.bimanual.title: Bimanual examination under anaesthesia
step.turbt.bimanual.why: A palpable or fixed mass suggests muscle-invasive or locally advanced disease, and this is the only moment it can be felt with the abdomen relaxed.
how: With the bladder empty, perform a bimanual examination before resection, and repeat it after resection.
Record whether a mass is palpable, mobile or fixed to the pelvic side wall.
pitfalls: Skipping it because the CT has been done; the two give complementary information.

step.turbt.resect.title: Resection of the exophytic tumour
step.turbt.resect.why: Removing the bulk first exposes the base and the stalk, and gives the pathologist the grade. Fractional or en bloc resection both aim for complete removal with orientation preserved.
how: Keep the bladder only partially filled so the wall is thicker and the tumour is close to the loop.
Resect the exophytic part in controlled strokes, or en bloc for suitable small tumours, using cutting current and minimal coagulation.
For lateral wall tumours, use short strokes and low energy, and stop if the obturator reflex appears.
pitfalls: Coagulating the tumour before resecting it, destroying the histology.

step.turbt.base.title: Base resection with detrusor muscle
step.turbt.base.why: Stage depends on whether the tumour invades the detrusor. A specimen without muscle cannot answer the question that decides between surveillance, intravesical therapy and cystectomy.
how: Resect the base of the tumour into the underlying muscle and send it as a separate specimen.
Biopsy the edges where the margin is unclear, and any suspicious flat red areas with cold-cup forceps.
Stop at muscle fibres; fat seen in the base means perforation.
pitfalls: A superficial base that misses muscle.
Mixing the base with the bulk tumour in one pot.

step.turbt.instillation.title: Immediate single post-operative chemotherapy instillation decision
step.turbt.instillation.why: A single early instillation reduces recurrence in appropriately selected tumours, but in a perforated or bleeding bladder it can cause serious extravesical toxicity.
how: Decide in theatre whether the patient meets the criteria in the current bladder cancer guideline.
Do not instil if a perforation is suspected or if continuous irrigation is needed for bleeding.
Prescribe it clearly with the time window, and hand over the clamping and drainage instructions to the ward nurses.
pitfalls: Instilling into a bladder with an unrecognised perforation.
The instillation being forgotten because nobody prescribed it in theatre.
